phy_ocra.20.0.summary: Light from distant galaxies is **red-shifted**: the dark lines in their spectra are moved towards the red (longer wavelength) end compared with the same lines measured in a lab or from the Sun. This tells us the galaxies are **moving away (receding)** from us, and the further away a galaxy is, the bigger its red-shift and so the **faster it is receding**. This pattern is evidence that the **universe is expanding**, which, together with the **cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR)**, supports the **Big Bang model**: the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense, small region and has been expanding and cooling ever since.

core.h: What is a spectrum and why do lines appear?
core.p: When white light from a star passes through the cooler gases in its outer layers, each element **absorbs particular wavelengths**. This leaves a pattern of dark lines (an **absorption spectrum**) on a continuous rainbow. Each element has its own unique pattern, like a barcode, so the pattern can be recognised in light from anywhere in the universe.
bullets: A spectrum spreads light out by wavelength: **violet/blue = short wavelength**, **red = long wavelength**.
Dark lines are at fixed wavelengths for a given element (for example hydrogen and helium).
Astronomers compare the line pattern from a galaxy with the same pattern measured in a laboratory or from the Sun.
The **spacing pattern** of the lines stays the same, which is how we know it is the same element even when the lines have moved.

callouts.p: Because the **pattern** of lines is recognisable, any shift in **position** of the whole pattern can be measured accurately.

core.p: In light from almost all distant galaxies the whole pattern of absorption lines is shifted towards the **red end** of the spectrum. The light reaching us has a **longer wavelength** and **lower frequency** than the light the galaxy emitted.
bullets: **Red-shift** = an observed increase in the wavelength of light from a galaxy, so spectral lines move towards the red end.
Wavelength increases, frequency decreases; the speed of light in a vacuum does not change.
The light does not literally become red; every line just moves along towards longer wavelength.
A source moving towards us would show **blue-shift** (shorter wavelength). A few very close galaxies such as Andromeda show this.

callouts.p: The increase in the observed wavelength of light from a galaxy that is moving away from us, so that the spectral lines are shifted towards the red end of the spectrum.

core.p: Think of a galaxy sending out wave crests as it moves away from us. Each new crest is emitted from a point slightly further away than the last, so the crests arrive **more spread out**. A larger gap between crests means a **longer wavelength**. This is the same idea as the pitch of an ambulance siren dropping as it drives away (the Doppler effect).
bullets: Source moving away: waves stretched, wavelength longer, **red-shift**.
Source moving towards: waves squashed, wavelength shorter, **blue-shift**.
The **faster** a galaxy recedes, the **greater** the change in wavelength.
OCR only needs this qualitatively: you will not be asked to calculate red-shift.

callouts.p: Say 'the galaxy is **moving away** (receding) so the **wavelength** of its light **increases**'. Mention wavelength, not just colour.

fig.cap: A galaxy moving away from Earth: each wave crest is emitted from further away, so the waves reaching us are stretched to a longer wavelength.

core.p: Astronomers (Edwin Hubble in the 1920s) measured the distances to galaxies and their red-shifts. They found that **more distant galaxies have bigger red-shifts**. A bigger red-shift means a higher recession speed, so **the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away**.
bullets: Recession speed is roughly **proportional to distance**: twice as far, about twice as fast.
A graph of speed against distance is a **straight line through the origin** (with some scatter from real data).
This pattern is seen in **every direction** we look.
Galaxies in all directions receding, with speed increasing with distance, is the key evidence that **space itself is expanding**.

callouts.p: Bigger red-shift, so faster recession; more distant galaxies have bigger red-shift, so more distant galaxies recede faster; so the universe is expanding.

core.h: Why this means the universe is expanding
core.p: If every galaxy is moving away from every other, and the further apart two galaxies are the faster they separate, then the space between them must be getting bigger. It is not that we are at the centre: **an observer in any galaxy would see the same thing**.
bullets: Model: dots drawn on a balloon. Inflate it and every dot moves away from every other dot.
Dots that start further apart separate faster, just like real galaxies.
There is **no special centre** on the surface: every dot sees the others receding.
Running the expansion **backwards in time**, everything must once have been much closer together.

callouts.p: Do not say the Earth or the Milky Way is at the centre of the universe. The same pattern would be seen from any galaxy.

fig.cap: As the universe expands, all galaxies (dots) move further apart from each other. Galaxies that were further apart separate by a larger distance in the same time, so they move apart faster.

core.p: The **Big Bang model** says the universe began about **13.8 billion years ago** from an **extremely small, extremely hot and extremely dense** region, and has been **expanding and cooling** ever since. It was not an explosion into existing space: space itself has been expanding.
bullets: Start: very small, very hot, very dense.
Since then: continual **expansion** and **cooling**.
As it cooled, particles, then atoms (mostly hydrogen and helium), then stars and galaxies formed.
Red-shift shows the expansion today; running it backwards points to a hot dense beginning.
The age of the universe can be estimated from how fast galaxies are receding and how far away they are.

callouts.p: The theory that the universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding (and cooling) ever since.

core.p: The second major piece of evidence is the **cosmic microwave background radiation**. Shortly after the Big Bang the universe was filled with very high energy radiation. As space expanded, this radiation was **stretched (red-shifted)** to much longer wavelengths, and today it arrives as **microwaves** from **every direction** in the sky.
bullets: CMBR is microwave radiation coming almost **uniformly from all directions**.
It was predicted by the Big Bang model before it was discovered (found by accident in 1965).
It is the left-over radiation from the hot early universe, stretched to microwave wavelengths by the expansion.
It corresponds to a very cold temperature today, about 2.7 K (around -270 °C), showing the universe has cooled.
The rival **Steady State** theory could not explain the CMBR, which is why most scientists accepted the Big Bang.

callouts.p: Learn both: (1) **red-shift of galaxies increasing with distance** and (2) the **CMBR**.

core.p: Scientific models are accepted when they explain the evidence and make predictions that are tested. The Steady State model also accepted expansion, but claimed new matter was continually created so the universe always looked the same and had no beginning.
bullets: Both models explain red-shift (expansion).
Only the Big Bang predicted the **CMBR**; Steady State could not explain it.
So when the CMBR was discovered, the Big Bang became the accepted model.
This is a good example of how **new evidence** changes which theory scientists accept.

core.h: How light carries information across the universe
core.p: Almost everything we know about distant galaxies comes from the electromagnetic radiation they send us. Spectra tell us **what elements** are present and, from the shift of the lines, **how fast** the source is moving towards or away from us.
bullets: Light from distant galaxies has travelled for millions or billions of years, so we see them **as they were** in the past.
Telescopes on Earth and in space collect light and other wavelengths (radio, microwave, X-ray).
Space telescopes avoid absorption and distortion by the atmosphere.
Measuring distance is harder than measuring red-shift, so distance data have more uncertainty, which is why real graphs show scatter.

core.p: The Big Bang model is the best explanation we have, but there are things it does not yet fully explain. Scientists keep testing it with new observations.
bullets: Observations suggest the expansion is actually **accelerating**, which is not fully understood.
Galaxies rotate faster than the visible matter can explain, suggesting extra unseen mass (often called **dark matter**).
We cannot observe what happened at the very first instant.
Distance measurements to the most distant galaxies have large uncertainties.

callouts.p: If asked why the Big Bang is accepted, say it explains **both** red-shift and the CMBR and **made a prediction** (the CMBR) that was later confirmed.

core.h: Linking the ideas in a 6-mark answer
core.p: Long answers reward a logical chain. Start with the observation, explain what it shows, then link it to the model.
bullets: Observation: spectral lines from distant galaxies are shifted to the red end (longer wavelength).
Meaning: the galaxies are moving away from us.
Pattern: more distant galaxies have a greater red-shift, so are moving away faster.
Conclusion: the universe is expanding; going back in time it was once very small, hot and dense.
Second evidence: CMBR, radiation left over from the early universe, now stretched to microwaves and coming from all directions.
Judgement: the Big Bang explains both; Steady State cannot explain the CMBR.

analogy.p: Picture a lump of dough with raisins in it rising in a warm oven. As the dough expands, every raisin moves away from every other raisin, and raisins that started further apart end up separating faster, because there is more dough between them to stretch. A raisin cannot tell it is not at the centre: from any raisin, all the others seem to rush away. The dough is space and the raisins are galaxies. Where it breaks down: a loaf has an edge and a centre and expands into the kitchen, but the universe is not expanding into anything and has no centre. Also the raisins themselves do not stretch, just as galaxies held together by gravity do not expand.

terms.d: The range of wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation, with light spread out from violet (short wavelength) to red (long wavelength).
A continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines where particular wavelengths have been absorbed by elements in a cooler gas.
Lines at fixed wavelengths characteristic of a particular element, forming a unique pattern.
The observed increase in wavelength (decrease in frequency) of light from a receding galaxy, shifting spectral lines towards the red end.
The observed decrease in wavelength of light from a source moving towards the observer.
Moving away from the observer.
The speed at which a galaxy is moving away from us; greater for more distant galaxies.
A huge group of billions of stars held together by gravity, such as the Milky Way.
The idea that space itself is stretching so that galaxies are getting further apart from each other.
The theory that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from a very small, very hot, very dense region and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
Microwave radiation reaching us almost uniformly from all directions, left over from the hot early universe and stretched by expansion.
An alternative theory in which the universe has no beginning and always looks the same, with new matter continually created as it expands.
The change in observed wavelength and frequency of a wave because the source is moving relative to the observer.
The distance light travels in one year, used for distances to stars and galaxies.

exam.q: State what is meant by red-shift.
model: Increase in (observed) wavelength of light from a galaxy / lines shifted to red end of the spectrum.

exam.q: What does the red-shift of light from a galaxy tell us about the motion of that galaxy?
model: It is moving away from us (receding).

exam.q: Galaxy A has a greater red-shift than galaxy B. Compare the two galaxies.
model: Galaxy A is moving away faster.
Galaxy A is (probably) further away.

exam.q: Explain how scientists know that the dark lines in a galaxy's spectrum have been shifted.
model: Compare with the spectrum of the same element measured in a lab / the Sun.
Same pattern of lines appears at longer wavelengths.

exam.q: Describe the relationship between the distance to a galaxy and its speed of recession, and state what this suggests.
model: Speed is (directly) proportional to distance / further galaxies move away faster.
Universe is expanding.
exam.tip: Proportional is the best word if the graph is a straight line through the origin.

exam.q: What is the cosmic microwave background radiation and why is it evidence for the Big Bang?
model: Microwave radiation coming from all directions in space.
Left over from the hot early universe.
Stretched/red-shifted to microwave wavelengths by expansion.
Predicted by Big Bang model / cannot be explained by Steady State.
exam.tip: Four marks: what it is, where it came from, why microwave, why it supports the theory.

exam.q: Explain why light from a receding galaxy has a longer wavelength when it reaches Earth.
model: Each wave crest is emitted from further away as the galaxy moves.
So crests are further apart / waves stretched, wavelength increases.

exam.q: Suggest why the Big Bang model replaced the Steady State model.
model: Discovery of CMBR.
Big Bang predicted/explains it but Steady State cannot.
exam.tip: Mention a specific piece of evidence.

exam.q: Describe the Big Bang model of the origin of the universe.
model: Universe began from a very small, very hot, very dense region (about 13.8 billion years ago).
It has been expanding and cooling since.
exam.tip: Hot, dense and expanding are the key words.

exam.q: Explain how observations of light from distant galaxies and other evidence support the Big Bang model.
model: Spectral lines from distant galaxies shifted to the red end / longer wavelength.
Shows galaxies are moving away.
More distant galaxies have greater red-shift, so move away faster.
So universe is expanding; seen in all directions.
Running back in time, universe was once very small, hot and dense.
CMBR from all directions, left-over radiation from early universe, explained only by Big Bang.
exam.tip: Build a chain: observation, meaning, pattern, conclusion, second evidence.

worked.q: A hydrogen line measured in a lab has a wavelength of 656 nm. The same line in light from galaxy X is at 670 nm and from galaxy Y at 700 nm. Which galaxy is further away? Explain.
steps: Shift for X = 670 - 656 = 14 nm towards longer wavelength.
Shift for Y = 700 - 656 = 44 nm.
Both are red-shifted, so both galaxies are receding.
Y has the bigger red-shift, so it is receding faster.
Since recession speed increases with distance, Y is further away.
worked.ans: Galaxy Y, because it has the larger red-shift so is moving away faster, and faster-receding galaxies are further away.

worked.q: A student says 'every galaxy is moving away from us, so we must be at the centre of the universe'. Write a model reply.
steps: Red-shift is seen in all directions, so galaxies are receding from us.
But the expansion is of space itself, like dots on an inflating balloon.
From any dot, all other dots move away, with further dots moving faster.
So an observer in any galaxy would see the same pattern.
worked.ans: We are not at the centre: in an expanding universe every galaxy sees all others receding, so the observation does not single us out.

worked.q: Explain why radiation released in the early universe is detected today as microwaves.
steps: The early universe was extremely hot, so the radiation had very short wavelengths and high energy.
Since then space has expanded.
The expansion stretched the radiation, increasing its wavelength (red-shift).
Over about 13.8 billion years the wavelength has grown into the microwave region.
worked.ans: Expansion of space has stretched (red-shifted) the original high-energy radiation to microwave wavelengths: the CMBR.

phy_ocra.20.1.summary: Stars form when **gravity** pulls a cloud of dust and gas (a **nebula**) together; as it collapses it heats up until the core is hot and dense enough for **nuclear fusion** of hydrogen nuclei into helium, releasing huge amounts of energy. A star is stable on the **main sequence** because the inward pull of **gravity** is balanced by the outward **pressure** from the hot gas and radiation produced by fusion. When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the balance is lost and the star's fate depends on its **mass**: Sun-sized stars become **red giants** then **white dwarfs**, while much more massive stars become **red supergiants** that explode as **supernovae**, leaving a **neutron star** or a **black hole**.

core.p: Every star begins inside a **nebula**, a huge cloud of **dust and gas** (mostly hydrogen, with some helium). The particles attract each other by **gravity**. Where the cloud is slightly denser, gravity pulls more material in, so the clump grows and pulls in even more.
bullets: Nebula = cloud of dust and gas in space.
Gravity is the force that starts star formation.
Clumps contract and become denser.
One nebula can form many stars (a star cluster).

callouts.p: A cloud of dust and gas (mainly hydrogen) in space from which stars form.

core.p: As the cloud collapses, **gravitational potential energy** is transferred into the **kinetic energy** of the particles, so the **temperature rises**. The hot, dense ball of gas is called a **protostar**. It glows but is not yet a true star because fusion has not started.
bullets: Collapse makes particles move faster: temperature increases.
Density and pressure in the centre increase.
When the core is hot enough (millions of degrees) and dense enough, hydrogen nuclei collide fast enough to **fuse**.
Fusion starting marks the birth of a star.

callouts.p: Particles falling inwards speed up; faster particles mean a higher temperature.

core.p: In the core, **hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium nuclei**. Nuclei are positively charged and repel, so they only fuse at extremely **high temperature and pressure**, where they move fast enough and collide often enough to overcome the repulsion. Fusion releases a large amount of energy, which is what makes stars shine.
bullets: Fusion = joining **light nuclei** to make a heavier nucleus.
Main fuel: hydrogen to helium.
The mass of the products is slightly **less** than the mass of the starting nuclei; the missing mass is released as energy.
Energy escapes as electromagnetic radiation (light, infrared, ultraviolet) and heats the star.
Fusion is **not** the same as fission (splitting heavy nuclei).

callouts.p: The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.

core.p: For most of its life a star is a stable **main sequence star**. It neither collapses nor blows apart because two effects are **balanced**: **gravity** pulls all the matter **inwards**, while the high temperature from fusion creates **outward pressure** (from the hot gas and the radiation).
bullets: Inward: gravitational attraction of the star's own mass.
Outward: pressure from thermal expansion of the hot gas and radiation pressure from fusion energy.
Balanced, so the star is in **equilibrium** and stays roughly the same size.
If fusion speeds up, the star heats and expands slightly, which cools it and slows fusion: it is self-regulating.
Our Sun has been on the main sequence for about 4.6 billion years and has roughly as long again to go.

callouts.p: Main sequence star: inward force of **gravity** balanced by outward **pressure** caused by energy released from **fusion**.

core.p: A star's **mass** decides how fast it uses its fuel and how it ends. More mass means stronger gravity, so the core is squeezed harder, becoming hotter and denser, so fusion runs much faster. Massive stars are brighter but have **shorter lives**.
bullets: Bigger mass: hotter core, faster fusion, shorter life.
Sun-sized stars: main sequence lasts about 10 billion years.
Very massive stars may last only a few million years.
The end stage is decided by mass.

core.h: When the hydrogen runs out: red giants
core.p: When the hydrogen in the core is used up, fusion in the core slows, so the outward pressure drops and **gravity wins**: the core **contracts** and heats up. This heats the surrounding layers so hydrogen fuses in a **shell** around the core and helium fuses in the core into heavier elements such as carbon. The extra energy makes the outer layers **expand** a lot and cool, so the surface looks red.
bullets: Sun-sized star becomes a **red giant**.
Massive star becomes a **red supergiant**.
Red because the expanded surface is cooler.
Inside, heavier elements are made by fusion of helium and beyond.

callouts.p: A red giant is red because its surface is **cooler**, not because it is hotter. Its core is hotter than before.

core.h: The end of a Sun-sized star
core.p: A red giant eventually becomes unstable and puffs off its outer layers into space (as a glowing cloud). The hot core left behind is a **white dwarf**: small, very dense and very hot, but no fusion happens in it. Over a very long time it cools and fades to a **black dwarf**.
bullets: Red giant sheds its outer layers.
Remaining core = **white dwarf**, about the size of the Earth.
No fusion: it just radiates its stored energy and cools.
Eventually becomes a cold **black dwarf** that gives out no visible light.

core.h: The end of a massive star: supernova
core.p: In a red supergiant, fusion builds heavier and heavier elements up to iron. Fusing iron does not release energy, so fusion stops, the core collapses under gravity in a fraction of a second, and the star explodes as a **supernova**. A supernova can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.
bullets: Fusion in massive stars makes elements up to **iron**.
Elements **heavier than iron** are made in the supernova explosion.
The explosion scatters these elements into space as a new nebula.
New stars and planets (including Earth and us) form from this material.

callouts.p: Light elements up to iron: fusion inside stars. Heavier than iron: supernovae.

core.p: After a supernova the core that remains is crushed by gravity. If it is massive enough it becomes a **neutron star**; if it is even more massive, gravity is so strong that it collapses to a **black hole**.
bullets: **Neutron star**: extremely dense, made almost entirely of neutrons; a teaspoon would weigh millions of tonnes.
**Black hole**: gravity so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
Black holes cannot be seen directly; they are detected by their effect on nearby matter and light.
Which one forms depends on the mass of the remaining core.

core.p: The whole life cycle can be explained as a contest between **gravity (inwards)** and **pressure (outwards)**. Each change of stage happens when the balance shifts.
bullets: Nebula to protostar: gravity wins, so the cloud collapses and heats.
Main sequence: fusion pressure balances gravity, so stable.
Red giant: core hydrogen runs out, core contracts, outer layers expand.
White dwarf: no fusion; gravity is held back by the particles being packed so closely.
Supernova: core collapse when fusion can no longer supply energy.
Black hole: gravity wins completely.

callouts.p: Describe stages in order and give the **reason** for each change in terms of gravity, temperature and fusion.

core.p: Fusion energy travels out from the core and leaves the surface as **electromagnetic radiation**. The colour of a star links to its surface temperature: hotter stars look blue-white, cooler stars look red.
bullets: Energy store in the nucleus is transferred to thermal energy and then radiation.
Hotter surface: peak emission at shorter wavelength (bluer).
Cooler surface: peak emission at longer wavelength (redder).
This is why a red giant's large, cooler surface looks red.

analogy.t: A balloon in a tug of war
analogy.p: A main sequence star is like a balloon: the rubber is always trying to squeeze inwards (gravity), while the air inside pushes outwards (pressure from the hot gas and radiation). The balloon stays the same size while the two balance. Heat the air (more fusion) and it swells; let it cool (fuel runs out in the core) and it shrinks. Where it breaks down: a balloon's air is not producing its own energy, while a star's core makes energy by fusion; and in a star the 'squeeze' comes from the star's own mass attracting itself, not from a stretched skin.

terms.d: A cloud of dust and gas, mostly hydrogen, from which stars form.
The attractive force between masses; it pulls a nebula together and pulls a star's matter inwards.
A hot, dense collapsing ball of gas that has not yet started fusion.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
A stable star fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, with gravity balanced by outward pressure.
The state where the inward force of gravity is balanced by outward pressure, so the star stays the same size.
The outward push from the energy (radiation) released by fusion in the core.
A large, cool-surfaced star formed when a Sun-sized star runs out of hydrogen in its core.
An extremely large star formed when a massive star runs out of hydrogen in its core.
The small, dense, hot core left after a red giant sheds its outer layers; no fusion takes place.
A white dwarf that has cooled so much it no longer emits significant light.
The explosion of a massive star after its core collapses, producing elements heavier than iron.
The extremely dense remnant of a supernova, made mostly of neutrons.
A remnant so dense that its gravity stops anything, including light, escaping.

mistakes.r: Fusion: light nuclei join together. Fission is splitting heavy nuclei.

mistakes.r: It heats up as gravity makes it collapse (gravitational potential energy to thermal); fusion starts later.

exam.q: Name the cloud of dust and gas from which a star forms.
model: Nebula.

exam.q: Name the force that causes a nebula to collapse.
model: Gravity / gravitational attraction.

exam.q: Explain why a protostar heats up.
model: Gravity causes it to collapse/contract.
Gravitational potential energy transferred to kinetic/thermal energy of particles, so temperature rises.

exam.q: Describe the nuclear process that releases energy in a main sequence star.
model: Nuclear fusion.
Hydrogen nuclei join to form helium nuclei (releasing energy).

exam.q: Explain why fusion only happens at very high temperatures.
model: Nuclei are positively charged and repel.
High temperature means high speed so they can collide hard enough to overcome repulsion and fuse.

exam.q: Explain why a main sequence star remains stable for billions of years.
model: Gravity pulls matter inwards.
Fusion in the core releases energy.
Causing outward pressure (thermal/radiation).
Forces balanced so star in equilibrium / size stays constant.
exam.tip: Name both forces and say they balance.

exam.q: State what happens to a Sun-sized star after its main sequence stage.
model: Becomes a red giant.
Then (sheds outer layers and) becomes a white dwarf.

exam.q: Explain why a red giant forms when the hydrogen in a star's core runs out.
model: Fusion in core slows, so outward pressure falls and core contracts and heats.
Fusion in shell/heavier elements releases more energy so outer layers expand (and cool).

exam.q: Where are elements heavier than iron made?
model: In a supernova (explosion).
exam.tip: Not in the core of a main sequence star.

exam.q: Describe the life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun, from its formation to its final stage. Include reasons for the changes.
model: Nebula of dust and gas pulled together by gravity.
Collapse heats it to form a protostar.
When hot/dense enough, fusion of hydrogen to helium starts: main sequence.
Gravity balanced by outward pressure from fusion energy.
Hydrogen runs out: becomes red supergiant, fusing heavier elements up to iron.
Core collapses, supernova; leaves neutron star or (if massive enough) black hole.
exam.tip: Order plus a reason at each change.

worked.q: Star P has 10 times the mass of the Sun. Star Q has the same mass as the Sun. Compare their life cycles.
steps: Both form from a nebula, become protostars, then main sequence stars.
P has stronger gravity, so a hotter, denser core: it fuses hydrogen much faster and so has a shorter main sequence life.
When core hydrogen runs out, Q becomes a red giant, P a red supergiant.
Q sheds its outer layers to leave a white dwarf.
P explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star (or a black hole if the core is massive enough).
worked.ans: Same start; P lives a shorter life and ends in a supernova with a neutron star or black hole, while Q ends as a white dwarf.

worked.q: Explain what would happen to a main sequence star if the rate of fusion in its core suddenly increased.
steps: More fusion releases more energy, so the core temperature rises.
Outward pressure becomes greater than gravity.
The star expands.
Expansion cools the core, so fusion slows back down.
The forces balance again at a slightly larger size.
worked.ans: The star expands until the forces balance again; this self-regulation keeps a main sequence star stable.

worked.q: A student says 'the iron in your blood was made in the Sun'. Evaluate this claim.
steps: Iron is made by fusion only in the cores of massive stars late in their life.
The Sun is a Sun-sized main sequence star fusing hydrogen to helium; it has not made iron.
Supernovae of earlier massive stars scattered iron into the nebula from which the Solar System formed.
worked.ans: Incorrect: the iron was made in earlier massive stars and spread by supernovae before the Sun and Earth formed.

phy_ocra.20.2.summary: **All bodies emit electromagnetic radiation**, whatever their temperature, and they emit a **range of wavelengths**. The **hotter** a body is, the **greater the intensity** of the radiation it emits and the **shorter the wavelength** at which the emission peaks, which is why a heated metal glows red, then yellow, then white. A body's temperature stays **constant** when it **absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it**; it warms up if it absorbs faster than it emits and cools down if it emits faster. The **Earth's temperature** depends on this balance between incoming radiation from the Sun and infrared radiation emitted into space, with the atmosphere and its greenhouse gases affecting how much infrared escapes.

core.p: Every object, from a star to an ice cube, emits **electromagnetic radiation** because of its temperature. At everyday temperatures most of this is **infrared**, which we cannot see. Only very hot objects (around 800 °C or more) emit enough visible light to glow.
bullets: Emission happens at **all temperatures** above absolute zero.
Objects also **absorb** radiation that falls on them (and may reflect or transmit some).
Your body (about 37 °C) emits mostly infrared, which is how thermal imaging cameras see people in the dark.
The Sun (surface about 5500 °C) emits mostly visible light plus infrared and ultraviolet.

callouts.p: All bodies emit and absorb radiation all the time. A cold object still emits, just less, and at longer wavelengths.

core.p: An object does not emit a single wavelength. It emits a **continuous range (distribution)** of wavelengths, with the most energy at one **peak wavelength**. On a graph of intensity against wavelength this gives a hump-shaped curve.
bullets: **Intensity** = power of radiation per unit area (how much energy arrives each second on each square metre).
The curve rises steeply, peaks, then falls slowly towards long wavelengths.
The **position of the peak** and the **height of the curve** both depend on the temperature.
Area under the curve relates to total power emitted.

core.p: As an object gets **hotter**, two things change: it emits **more radiation at every wavelength** (higher intensity, much more total power) and the **peak shifts to shorter wavelengths**. So a hotter object gives out a larger share of visible and even ultraviolet radiation.
bullets: Hotter: **higher intensity** at all wavelengths.
Hotter: **peak wavelength shorter** (shifts towards blue/violet).
Cooler: lower intensity, peak at longer wavelength (towards infrared).
Glowing metal: dull red, then orange, then yellow-white as it heats up.
Star colours: red stars are cooler; blue-white stars are hotter.

head: Object
Approx. temperature
Peak emission
rows: Infrared, with a lot of visible

callouts.p: Hotter objects do not only emit short wavelengths. They emit **more at all wavelengths**, but the **peak** moves to shorter wavelength.

fig.cap: Intensity against wavelength for bodies at 3000 K, 4000 K and 5000 K. The hotter body emits more radiation at every wavelength and its peak is at a shorter wavelength.

core.p: How fast a surface absorbs and emits radiation depends on its colour and texture as well as its temperature. A **perfect black body** absorbs all radiation that hits it and is also the best possible emitter.
bullets: **Dark, matt** surfaces are good absorbers **and** good emitters.
**Light, shiny** surfaces are poor absorbers and poor emitters; they are good reflectors.
A good absorber is always a good emitter at the same temperature.
Examples: solar panels are black; emergency blankets and kettles are shiny; houses in hot countries are painted white.

callouts.p: An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it; it does not reflect or transmit any, and it is the best possible emitter.

core.p: A common practical uses a metal cube with four different faces (matt black, shiny black, matt white, shiny silver), filled with hot water. An infrared detector (or thermometer) is placed the **same distance** from each face to compare the radiation emitted.
bullets: Independent variable: type of surface.
Dependent variable: reading on the infrared detector.
Control variables: same temperature of water, same distance from face, same detector.
Result: matt black face gives the highest reading; shiny silver the lowest.
Safety: hot water; handle the cube with care.

callouts.p: Always say the detector is the **same distance** from each face, and readings are taken at the **same time** so the water temperature is the same.

core.p: Whether something heats up or cools down depends on the **balance** between the **rate it absorbs radiation** and the **rate it emits radiation** (plus any other energy transfers). Temperature only stays constant when these rates are equal.
bullets: Absorbs faster than it emits: **temperature rises**.
Absorbs and emits at the **same rate**: **temperature constant**.
Emits faster than it absorbs: **temperature falls**.
As an object warms up, it emits more, so it reaches a new balance at a higher temperature.
This is why objects do not keep heating up forever in sunlight.

callouts.p: Constant temperature means **rate of absorption = rate of emission**.

fig.cap: Three cases of energy balance. If radiation is absorbed faster than it is emitted the object warms; equal rates keep the temperature steady; emitting faster than absorbing makes it cool.

core.p: The same idea explains many everyday situations. Look for what is absorbed, what is emitted and which is bigger.
bullets: A cup of tea cools because it emits (and loses by other means) more energy than it absorbs from the cooler room; it cools faster at first because a hotter object emits more.
It stops cooling when it reaches room temperature: absorbing and emitting at the same rate.
A car in sunshine heats up until it emits as fast as it absorbs; a dark car reaches a higher temperature.
A clear night is colder than a cloudy one: clouds absorb infrared from the ground and emit some back.
A greenhouse lets visible light in; the warmed contents emit infrared, some of which the glass absorbs and re-emits inwards.

core.p: The Sun is very hot, so its radiation peaks in the **visible** region, with some **ultraviolet** and **infrared**. Most of this short-wavelength radiation passes through the atmosphere.
bullets: Some is **reflected** back into space by clouds, ice, snow and the atmosphere.
Some is **absorbed** by the atmosphere (for example ozone absorbs much of the UV).
The rest is **absorbed by the Earth's surface**, which warms up.
Light surfaces such as ice reflect more; dark oceans and forests absorb more.

core.p: The Earth's surface is much **cooler** than the Sun, so it emits radiation at **longer wavelengths**, mostly **infrared**. This difference in wavelength is the key to the greenhouse effect.
bullets: Incoming: mainly **short-wavelength** (visible) radiation from the very hot Sun.
Outgoing: mainly **long-wavelength infrared** from the cool Earth.
Some infrared passes straight out to space.
Some is **absorbed by greenhouse gases** in the atmosphere.

callouts.p: The Sun is hot so it emits short wavelengths; the Earth is cool so it emits long-wavelength infrared.

The surface emits infrared; some escapes to space, while greenhouse gases absorb some and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the surface.

core.p: **Greenhouse gases** such as **carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour** let most of the incoming short-wavelength radiation through but **absorb** the outgoing **infrared**. They then **re-emit** infrared in **all directions**, some of it back towards the Earth. This means less energy escapes to space, so the Earth is warmer than it would otherwise be.
bullets: Without any greenhouse effect, the average surface temperature would be far below freezing (roughly -18 °C instead of about 15 °C).
The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life.
Increasing greenhouse gas concentration (burning fossil fuels, farming, deforestation) means more infrared is absorbed and re-emitted back.
Energy is then emitted to space more slowly than it is absorbed, so the Earth warms.
It warms until it emits enough to balance again, at a **higher equilibrium temperature**: this is **global warming**.

callouts.p: Greenhouse gases do not 'trap heat' in a lid, and the effect is not caused by the ozone hole. They **absorb and re-emit infrared**.

core.h: Factors that change the Earth's temperature
core.p: Anything that changes the **rate of absorption** or the **rate of emission to space** changes the Earth's equilibrium temperature.
bullets: More greenhouse gases: less infrared escapes, temperature rises.
Less ice and snow: less sunlight reflected, more absorbed, temperature rises (which melts more ice: a positive feedback).
More cloud: reflects more sunlight (cooling) but also absorbs and re-emits infrared (warming).
Large volcanic eruptions: dust reflects sunlight, temporary cooling.
Changes in the Sun's output also change the incoming radiation.

callouts.p: Incoming radiation, what happens to it, outgoing infrared, role of greenhouse gases, balance idea, effect of a change.

analogy.t: A bath with the tap on and the plug out
analogy.p: Think of the Earth's temperature as the water level in a bath. The tap is the incoming radiation from the Sun and the plughole is the infrared escaping to space. The level stays steady when water flows in as fast as it drains out. Greenhouse gases are like partly blocking the plughole: the level rises until the extra pressure makes water drain fast enough to balance the tap again, at a higher level. Where it breaks down: the 'drain' from a real object increases strongly with temperature in a way a plughole does not exactly copy, and greenhouse gases do not remove energy: they absorb infrared and re-emit it in all directions, sending some back to the surface.

terms.d: Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves, such as infrared, visible light and ultraviolet.
Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light, emitted strongly by warm objects.
The power of radiation per unit area.
The wavelength at which a body emits radiation with the greatest intensity; shorter for hotter bodies.
The spread of intensity across the different wavelengths emitted by a body.
When radiation is taken in by a material, transferring energy to it.
When a body gives out radiation.
An object that absorbs all radiation incident on it and is the best possible emitter.
The state where a body absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits it, so its temperature is constant.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide, methane or water vapour, that absorbs infrared radiation and re-emits it.
The warming of the Earth because greenhouse gases absorb infrared emitted by the surface and re-emit some back towards it.
The rise in the Earth's average temperature caused by increased greenhouse gas concentrations.
When radiation bounces off a surface without being absorbed.
How much of the incoming radiation a surface reflects; ice reflects a lot, oceans very little.

mistakes.w: Only hot objects emit radiation.
mistakes.r: All bodies emit radiation; cooler bodies emit less and at longer wavelengths.

mistakes.w: Hotter objects emit longer wavelengths.
mistakes.r: Hotter objects have a peak at shorter wavelength (and higher intensity).

mistakes.w: An object stays at the same temperature because it stops emitting.
mistakes.r: It still emits; temperature is constant because absorption and emission rates are equal.

mistakes.w: Black surfaces are good absorbers but poor emitters.
mistakes.r: Dark matt surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters.

mistakes.w: Greenhouse gases trap the Sun's rays.
mistakes.r: They absorb infrared emitted by the Earth and re-emit it, some back towards the surface.

mistakes.w: The greenhouse effect is caused by the hole in the ozone layer.
mistakes.r: Ozone absorbs UV; the greenhouse effect is absorption of infrared by gases like CO2 and methane.

mistakes.w: The Earth emits the same radiation it receives from the Sun.
mistakes.r: The Earth is cooler, so it emits longer-wavelength infrared.

mistakes.w: Global warming means the Earth absorbs more sunlight because of greenhouse gases.
mistakes.r: Greenhouse gases mainly reduce the rate infrared escapes, so the Earth warms to a new higher balance temperature.

exam.q: State which objects emit electromagnetic radiation.
model: All objects / all bodies (at any temperature).
exam.tip: Do not say only hot objects.

exam.q: Describe how the radiation emitted by an object changes as its temperature increases.
model: Intensity / total energy emitted increases.
Peak wavelength decreases / shifts to shorter wavelength.
exam.tip: Two changes: how much and which wavelength.

exam.q: A metal rod is heated and glows red, then yellow-white. Explain the change in colour.
model: As temperature increases peak shifts to shorter wavelength.
So more of the shorter visible wavelengths (yellow, green, blue) are emitted, mixing to look white.

exam.q: State the condition for an object to remain at a constant temperature.
model: It absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits radiation.

exam.q: Explain why a cup of hot tea cools quickly at first and then more slowly.
model: Hotter tea emits radiation at a higher rate than it absorbs from the room.
As it cools the rate of emission falls, closer to rate of absorption, so cooling slows (stops at room temperature).

exam.q: Describe an experiment to compare the infrared radiation emitted by different surfaces.
model: Use a cube with different surfaces filled with hot water.
Place infrared detector/thermometer the same distance from each face.
Take readings at the same time/same water temperature.
Compare readings: matt black highest, shiny silver lowest.

exam.q: Explain why the radiation emitted by the Earth has a longer wavelength than the radiation it receives from the Sun.
model: The Earth is at a much lower temperature than the Sun.
Cooler objects emit with peak at longer wavelength (infrared).

exam.q: Name two greenhouse gases.
model: Carbon dioxide.
Methane / water vapour.
exam.tip: Oxygen and nitrogen are not greenhouse gases.

exam.q: Explain how greenhouse gases keep the Earth warmer than it would otherwise be.
model: Sun's (short-wavelength) radiation passes through atmosphere and is absorbed by surface.
Surface emits infrared (longer wavelength).
Greenhouse gases absorb some infrared.
And re-emit it in all directions, some back to Earth, so less energy lost to space.
exam.tip: Absorb and re-emit are the key verbs.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of radiation, why increasing the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere leads to a rise in the Earth's average temperature.
model: Earth's temperature is constant when rate of absorbing radiation equals rate of emitting to space.
Incoming radiation from the Sun is mostly short-wavelength, passing through atmosphere.
Earth's surface emits infrared because it is cooler.
More CO2 absorbs more of this infrared and re-emits it, some back to the surface.
So rate of energy lost to space falls below rate absorbed; Earth warms.
Warmer Earth emits more until balance restored at a higher temperature.
exam.tip: Finish with the new, higher equilibrium.

worked.q: Two identical cans, one painted matt black and one shiny silver, are filled with water at 20 °C and placed in sunlight. Predict and explain what happens to their temperatures.
steps: Both absorb radiation faster than they emit at first, so both warm up.
Matt black absorbs radiation at a greater rate than shiny silver.
So the black can warms faster.
As each warms, its emission rate rises until absorption = emission.
The black can reaches balance at a higher temperature than the silver can.
worked.ans: Both warm then level off; the black can warms faster and reaches a higher steady temperature.

worked.q: Star A is red and star B is blue-white. Which is hotter and how does its emission compare?
steps: Colour depends on the peak wavelength of emission.
Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light.
Shorter peak wavelength means a higher temperature.
A hotter body also emits more intensely at all wavelengths.
worked.ans: Star B is hotter: its peak is at a shorter wavelength and it emits more intensely (per unit area) at every wavelength.

worked.q: A large area of Arctic ice melts, revealing dark ocean. Explain the effect on the Earth's temperature.
steps: Ice is light and reflects much of the incoming sunlight.
Dark ocean absorbs much more of it.
So the rate of absorption increases while emission is unchanged at first.
Absorption is now greater than emission, so the temperature rises.
The Earth warms until it emits enough to balance again; the warming melts more ice (positive feedback).
worked.ans: More radiation is absorbed, so the Earth warms to a higher equilibrium temperature, which can melt more ice.

phy_ocra.20.3.summary: Our **solar system** is the **Sun** (a star) with everything that orbits it: **eight planets**, dwarf planets such as Pluto, **moons** (natural satellites of planets), **asteroids** and **comets**. Humans have also launched **artificial satellites** that orbit the Earth. All of these stay in orbit because **gravity** provides a force towards the centre of the orbit; in a circular orbit this force changes the **direction** of motion, so the **velocity changes** while the **speed stays the same**. For a **stable orbit** there is only one speed for each radius: **closer orbits must be faster**, so if an object's speed changes, the radius of its orbit must change too.

core.h: The main features of the solar system
core.p: The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a nebula. At its centre is the **Sun**, which contains over 99% of the mass of the solar system and is the only body that produces its own light by fusion. Everything else orbits the Sun because of its **gravity**.
bullets: **Sun**: a main sequence star at the centre.
**Eight planets**: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune (memory aid: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming).
**Dwarf planets** such as Pluto: orbit the Sun but have not cleared their orbit of other objects.
**Moons**: natural satellites orbiting planets.
**Asteroids**: small rocky bodies, many in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
**Comets**: lumps of ice and dust in very elongated (elliptical) orbits.
The solar system is part of the **Milky Way** galaxy.

callouts.p: An object that orbits a larger object. Moons are natural satellites; artificial satellites are made by humans.

core.p: The planets split into two groups. The **inner planets** are small, rocky and dense. The **outer planets** are **gas giants**, much bigger, made mainly of hydrogen and helium, with many moons and ring systems.
bullets: Inner: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars; rocky, few or no moons.
Outer: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune; gas giants, many moons, rings.
Further from the Sun: colder, and longer time to orbit (longer year).
All planets orbit in the **same direction** and roughly in the same plane.

core.h: Planets, moons and artificial satellites compared
core.p: Planets, moons and artificial satellites all move in orbits held by gravity, but they orbit different things and come from different origins.
bullets: **Similarity**: all are kept in orbit by gravity from the body at the centre of the orbit.
Planets orbit a **star** (the Sun); moons orbit a **planet**; artificial satellites usually orbit the **Earth**.
Orbits of planets and moons are **nearly circular**; comet orbits are very **elliptical**.
None of them produce their own light; we see them by reflected sunlight.
Artificial satellites are placed in chosen orbits for a purpose.

callouts.p: The Moon is a **natural satellite**, not an artificial one. And the Sun is a star, not a planet.

core.p: Without a force, an object would travel in a **straight line at constant speed** (Newton's first law). An orbiting body keeps curving round because **gravity pulls it towards the centre** of its orbit all the time. The object is continually 'falling' towards the central body but moving sideways fast enough that it keeps missing it.
bullets: Gravitational force acts **towards the centre** of the orbit.
This force is **perpendicular** to the direction of motion in a circular orbit.
A force towards the centre of a circle is called a **centripetal force**; gravity provides it.
If gravity suddenly disappeared, the object would fly off along a **tangent** in a straight line.

callouts.p: Gravity provides the force towards the centre that keeps a planet, moon or satellite in orbit.

core.p: **Speed** is a scalar: how fast. **Velocity** is a vector: speed **in a given direction**. In a circular orbit the speed stays the same, but the **direction keeps changing**, so the **velocity is always changing**. A changing velocity is an **acceleration**, and this acceleration is towards the centre, caused by the resultant force of gravity.
bullets: Gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so it does **no work** in the direction of motion and the speed does not change.
It only changes the **direction** of motion.
Changing direction means changing velocity, so the body is **accelerating** towards the centre.
Resultant force is not zero, so the orbiting object is **not** in equilibrium.

callouts.p: Speed in a given direction (a vector quantity).
'The speed is constant but the direction changes, so the velocity changes. Gravity provides the force towards the centre.'

core.p: Gravity gets **weaker with distance**. A body in a **smaller orbit** feels **stronger gravity**, so it needs to move **faster** to stay in a stable orbit rather than spiral in. A body in a **larger orbit** feels weaker gravity, so a stable orbit needs a **lower speed**. It also has further to go, so it takes **much longer** to complete one orbit.
bullets: Smaller radius: stronger gravity, **higher speed**, **shorter period**.
Larger radius: weaker gravity, **lower speed**, **longer period**.
Mercury orbits the Sun in 88 days; Neptune takes about 165 years.
Low Earth orbit satellites take about 90 minutes; the Moon takes about 27 days.

core.h: Why the radius must change if the speed changes
core.p: For a stable circular orbit, each radius has **one particular speed**. So if the speed of an orbiting object changes, it **cannot stay at the same radius**: it moves to a different orbit.
bullets: If the speed is **too low** for its radius, gravity pulls it inwards, so it moves to a **smaller orbit** (or falls in).
If the speed is **too high** for its radius, it moves outwards to a **larger orbit** (or escapes completely if fast enough).
A satellite slowed by drag from the thin upper atmosphere gradually drops to lower orbits and may burn up.
Rocket engines are used to change a satellite's speed in order to move it to a new orbit.
OCR only needs this qualitatively: no orbital calculations.

callouts.p: Stable orbit: closer means faster. Change the speed and the radius must change.

core.p: Comets have highly **elliptical** (stretched) orbits. Their distance from the Sun changes a lot, so the strength of gravity changes, and so does their speed.
bullets: Closest to the Sun: gravity strongest, comet moves **fastest**.
Furthest from the Sun: gravity weakest, comet moves **slowest**.
Near the Sun, ice evaporates to form the glowing tail, which points away from the Sun.
This fits the same rule: closer orbit position means higher speed.

core.p: Artificial satellites are put into orbits chosen for their job. Two important types are **geostationary** and **polar** orbits.
bullets: **Geostationary**: high orbit (about 36 000 km) above the **equator**; period **24 hours**, same direction as Earth spins, so it stays above the **same point** on the Earth. Used for **communications** and TV, as dishes can point at a fixed spot.

**Polar (low) orbit**: passes over the **poles**, a few hundred km up, period about **90 to 100 minutes**. As the Earth turns underneath, it scans the **whole surface**. Used for **weather monitoring, mapping, imaging and spying**.
Other uses: GPS navigation, the International Space Station, space telescopes such as Hubble.

callouts.p: The low polar satellite moves faster than the high geostationary one: closer orbit, stronger gravity, higher speed.

core.p: Exam questions often combine features of the solar system with the physics of orbits. Use the same reasoning for any orbiting object.
bullets: Identify what is being orbited (star, planet, Earth).
Gravity from that body provides the force towards the centre.
Circular orbit: speed constant, velocity changing, acceleration towards centre.
Closer means stronger gravity, faster speed and shorter period.
A change in speed means a change in orbital radius.

callouts.p: Astronauts on the ISS are not weightless because there is no gravity: gravity there is still about 90% of that on Earth. They are in continuous free fall around the Earth.

analogy.t: A ball whirled on a string
analogy.p: Whirl a ball on a string in a horizontal circle. The string pulls the ball towards your hand (like gravity pulling towards the Sun), so the ball keeps changing direction while going round at a steady speed. Let go and it flies off in a straight line along a tangent. Where it breaks down: the string's pull can be any size you choose, but gravity gets weaker with distance, which is why larger orbits must be slower; also a string can only pull when tight, while gravity acts across empty space without any contact.

terms.d: The Sun and all the objects that orbit it: planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
A large body that orbits a star and has cleared its orbit of other objects.
A body orbiting the Sun that is large enough to be round but has not cleared its orbit, such as Pluto.
A natural satellite that orbits a planet.
A human-made object placed in orbit, usually around the Earth.
A small rocky body orbiting the Sun, many in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.
A body of ice and dust in a highly elliptical orbit around the Sun.
The path of one body around another, held by gravity.
Distance travelled per unit time (a scalar).
Speed in a given direction (a vector).
A resultant force towards the centre of a circle that keeps an object moving in a circular path; gravity provides it for orbits.
The time taken to complete one orbit.
An orbit above the equator with a 24-hour period, so the satellite stays above the same point on Earth.
A low orbit passing over the North and South Poles, allowing the whole surface to be scanned as the Earth rotates.
A stretched, oval-shaped orbit in which the distance from the central body changes.

mistakes.w: In a circular orbit the velocity is constant.
mistakes.r: Speed is constant but direction changes, so velocity changes.

mistakes.w: An orbiting object is not accelerating because its speed is constant.
mistakes.r: It is accelerating towards the centre because its velocity (direction) is changing.

mistakes.w: There is no gravity in orbit.
mistakes.r: Gravity is what keeps the object in orbit; it provides the force towards the centre.

mistakes.w: Satellites further from Earth go faster.
mistakes.r: Further orbits have weaker gravity, so they are slower (and have longer periods).

mistakes.w: A satellite can speed up and stay in the same orbit.
mistakes.r: For a stable orbit, a change in speed requires a change in radius.

mistakes.w: The Moon is an artificial satellite.
mistakes.r: The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth.

mistakes.w: The force of gravity acts in the direction the planet is moving.
mistakes.r: Gravity acts towards the centre of the orbit, at right angles to the velocity.

mistakes.w: Geostationary satellites do not move.
mistakes.r: They orbit at the same rate the Earth spins (24 hours), so they stay above the same point.

exam.q: Name the force that keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
model: Gravity / gravitational force (of the Sun).

exam.q: State the difference between a moon and an artificial satellite.
model: A moon is natural / an artificial satellite is made by humans.
Moons orbit planets; artificial satellites (usually) orbit the Earth.

exam.q: Describe two differences between the inner and outer planets.
model: Inner are small and rocky; outer are large gas giants.
Outer have more moons / rings / longer orbital periods / colder.

exam.q: State the direction of the gravitational force on a planet in a circular orbit.
model: Towards the centre of the orbit (the Sun).

exam.q: Explain why a planet in a circular orbit is accelerating even though its speed is constant.
model: Its direction of motion is changing, so its velocity is changing.
Acceleration is change in velocity; caused by gravity towards the centre.

exam.q: Explain why the speed of a planet in a circular orbit does not change.
model: Gravity acts at right angles to the direction of motion.
So it changes only the direction, not the speed.

exam.q: Satellite X orbits closer to the Earth than satellite Y. Compare their speeds and orbital periods.
model: X moves faster (gravity stronger).
X has a shorter period.

exam.q: A satellite in a stable orbit is slowed down by air resistance. Explain what happens to its orbit.
model: Its speed is now too low for its orbital radius.
So gravity pulls it into a smaller orbit / it spirals inwards (and may burn up).

exam.q: Compare geostationary and polar orbits and explain how each suits its use.
model: Geostationary: high, above equator, 24 h period.
Stays above same point, so good for communications.
Polar: low, over the poles, short period (about 90 min).
Earth rotates beneath so it scans whole surface: weather/monitoring.

exam.q: Explain how gravity keeps the Moon in a circular orbit around the Earth and why the Moon's velocity changes but its speed does not. Include what would happen if the Moon's speed changed.
model: Earth's gravity pulls the Moon towards the centre of its orbit.
Without this force, the Moon would move in a straight line (tangent).
Force is at right angles to its motion, so it changes direction not speed.
Direction changes so velocity changes: the Moon accelerates towards the Earth.
For a stable orbit each radius has one speed; closer orbits need faster speeds.
If speed decreased it would move to a smaller orbit; if it increased it would move to a larger orbit.
exam.tip: Cover force, direction, velocity and the speed-radius link.

worked.q: A newly launched satellite is in a low orbit. Engineers want to move it to a much higher orbit. Will its final orbital speed be higher or lower? Explain.
steps: At a higher orbit, the satellite is further from the Earth.
Gravity is weaker at greater distance.
A weaker force towards the centre can only keep a slower object in a circular orbit.
So for a stable higher orbit the speed must be lower, and the period longer.
worked.ans: Lower: a higher stable orbit has weaker gravity, so the orbital speed must be lower (and the period longer).

worked.q: Halley's Comet has a very elliptical orbit. Describe how its speed changes during one orbit and explain why.
steps: As it moves towards the Sun, its distance decreases so gravity is stronger.
Gravity has a component along its motion, so it speeds up.
It is fastest at its closest point to the Sun.
Moving away, gravity slows it; it is slowest at its furthest point.
worked.ans: Fastest when closest to the Sun, slowest when furthest away, because the gravitational pull is stronger closer to the Sun.

worked.q: Mars takes about 1.9 Earth years to orbit the Sun and Jupiter about 12 years. Use ideas about orbits to explain why.
steps: Jupiter is much further from the Sun than Mars.
The Sun's gravity is weaker at Jupiter's distance, so its stable orbital speed is lower.
Jupiter also has a much longer orbit to travel round.
Lower speed and longer path both increase the time for one orbit.
worked.ans: Jupiter is further from the Sun, so it moves more slowly around a longer path, giving a much longer orbital period.

phy_ocra.20.4.summary: Earthquakes produce **seismic waves** that travel through the Earth and are detected by **seismometers** around the world. **P-waves** are **longitudinal**, faster, and travel through **solids and liquids**; **S-waves** are **transverse**, slower, and can travel **only through solids**. Because S-waves are never detected on the far side of the Earth (the **S-wave shadow zone**), the **outer core must be liquid**, and the way P-waves **refract** at the core boundary creates **P-wave shadow zones** that show the size of the core and suggest a **solid inner core**. Studying these waves gives evidence for the layered structure of the Earth: **crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core**.

core.p: The deepest hole ever drilled reaches only about 12 km, while the Earth's radius is about 6400 km. We cannot see inside the Earth, so scientists use **seismic waves** from earthquakes as a probe. How the waves travel, how fast, and where they are (or are not) detected tells us about the materials inside.
bullets: Earthquakes release energy that spreads out as seismic waves.
Waves are detected by **seismometers** at many stations on the surface.
Times of arrival and patterns of detection are compared worldwide.
Using waves to find out about hidden structures is also used in ultrasound scanning and sonar.

callouts.p: An instrument that detects and records the vibrations of seismic waves.

core.p: Seismic evidence shows the Earth has four main layers. Their thickness and state (solid or liquid) were worked out mainly from how P and S waves travel.
bullets: **Crust**: thin, solid, rocky outer layer (about 5 to 70 km thick).
**Mantle**: solid rock (it can flow very slowly), down to about 2900 km.
**Outer core**: **liquid** iron and nickel.
**Inner core**: **solid** iron and nickel, very hot and under enormous pressure.

fig.cap: Layers of the Earth: a thin solid crust, a thick solid mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Seismic waves provide the evidence for the outer core being liquid.

core.p: **P-waves** (primary waves) are **longitudinal**: the particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction the wave travels, producing compressions and rarefactions, like sound waves. Longitudinal waves can travel through **solids and liquids**.
bullets: Longitudinal.
**Faster** than S-waves, so they arrive first.
Travel through **solids and liquids** (and gases).
Can pass through the core.

callouts.p: A wave in which the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.

core.p: **S-waves** (secondary waves) are **transverse**: particles vibrate at **right angles** to the direction of travel. A transverse wave needs the material to resist being sheared sideways. **Liquids cannot do this**, so S-waves can travel **only through solids**.
bullets: Transverse.
**Slower** than P-waves, so they arrive second.
Travel through **solids only**.
Stopped by the liquid outer core.

callouts.p: A wave in which the vibrations are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of energy transfer.

fig.cap: S-waves are transverse (vibrations at right angles to the direction of travel); P-waves are longitudinal (vibrations parallel to the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions).

core.h: Seismic waves refract inside the Earth
core.p: The speed of seismic waves depends on the material they travel through. Inside the mantle the properties (density and stiffness) change **gradually** with depth, so the wave speed changes gradually and the waves follow **curved paths**. At a **boundary** between layers the speed changes **suddenly**, so the waves change direction sharply: this is **refraction**.
bullets: Change in speed causes a change in direction: **refraction**.
Gradual change in speed with depth: smoothly **curved** paths.
Sudden change at the mantle-core boundary: sharp bend.
P-waves **slow down** when they enter the liquid outer core, so they bend towards the normal.
Waves can also partly **reflect** at boundaries.

callouts.p: Curved paths show properties change gradually with depth; sudden changes in direction show sharp boundaries between layers.

core.p: After a large earthquake, S-waves are detected by seismometers on the near side of the Earth, but **no S-waves** reach a large area on the **opposite side**. This region is the **S-wave shadow zone** (more than about 105 degrees from the epicentre).
bullets: S-waves cannot travel through liquids.
So something in the Earth's centre must be **liquid**, blocking them.
The size of the shadow zone lets scientists calculate the **size of the liquid outer core**.
This is the key evidence that the **outer core is liquid**.

callouts.p: No S-waves on the opposite side of the Earth: S-waves cannot pass through liquid, so the **outer core is liquid**.

core.p: P-waves do pass through the core, but when they cross the mantle-core boundary their speed changes suddenly and they **refract**. This bends them away from certain regions, leaving **P-wave shadow zones**, rings at about **104 to 140 degrees** from the epicentre where hardly any P-waves are detected.
bullets: P-waves are detected close to the earthquake and again on the far side (beyond about 140 degrees).
The gap between is caused by **refraction** at the core boundary.
The positions of the shadow zones tell us the **size of the core**.
Weak P-waves detected inside the shadow zone are explained by reflection/refraction from a **solid inner core** with a different wave speed.
This is the evidence for a **solid inner core**.

callouts.p: The P-wave shadow zone is caused by **refraction**, not by P-waves being absorbed by the liquid. P-waves can travel through liquids.

core.h: Arrival times and locating an earthquake
core.p: P-waves travel faster than S-waves, so at any seismometer the P-waves arrive first. The **time gap** between the P and S arrivals increases with distance from the earthquake. Using distance = speed x time for each wave lets you calculate how far away the earthquake was.
bullets: Further from the earthquake: bigger time gap between P and S arrivals.
Each station works out its distance from the epicentre.
Draw a circle of that radius round each station on a map.
Using **three stations**, the circles cross at one point: the **epicentre**.
Wave equation also applies: wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda).

callouts.p: Use distance = speed x time. Convert km to m and minutes to seconds if needed, and check units in the answer.

core.p: Scientists did not assume the Earth's structure: they inferred it by comparing observations from thousands of seismometers with predictions from different models.
bullets: If the Earth were solid and uniform, waves would travel in straight lines and be detected everywhere: this is not what is seen.
Curved paths show increasing wave speed with depth in the mantle.
The S-wave shadow zone shows a liquid outer core.
The P-wave shadow zones show the core's size and refraction at its boundary.
P-waves detected in the shadow zone suggest a solid inner core.

core.h: Comparing with other waves you know
core.p: Seismic waves follow the same rules as all waves: they transfer **energy** without transferring matter, and they can be **reflected**, **refracted** and **absorbed**.
bullets: P-waves behave like sound waves (longitudinal, travel through solids, liquids and gases).
S-waves behave like waves on a rope (transverse).
Electromagnetic waves are also transverse but need no medium; seismic waves need a medium.
Wave speed = frequency x wavelength applies to all waves.

core.p: Questions often give a diagram of wave paths and ask you to explain what it shows about the Earth's structure. Link each observation to a property of P or S waves.
bullets: State the property: S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids; P-waves are longitudinal and can.
State the observation: S-wave shadow zone on the far side.
Conclude: outer core is liquid.
Explain P-wave shadow zone by refraction at the core boundary.
Mention curved paths as evidence of changing properties with depth.
Mention solid inner core from P-waves detected in the shadow zone.

callouts.p: Use the words **transverse**, **longitudinal**, **refraction**, **shadow zone** and **liquid outer core** explicitly.

analogy.t: Shining torches through a mystery box
analogy.p: Imagine trying to find out what is inside a sealed box by sending two kinds of probe through it: one that can pass through water and one that is blocked by water. If the second probe never comes out on the far side, there must be water in the middle. That is exactly how S-waves reveal the liquid outer core. And just as light bends and leaves a dark ring when it passes through a glass ball, P-waves bend at the core boundary and leave shadow zones. Where it breaks down: seismic waves are mechanical vibrations of rock, not light, and the Earth's layers change gradually as well as at sharp boundaries, so the paths curve rather than just bending at edges.

mistakes.r: P-waves travel through solids and liquids; it is S-waves that cannot travel through liquids.

mistakes.w: Seismic waves travel in straight lines through the Earth.
mistakes.r: They follow curved paths because their speed changes gradually with depth (refraction).

mistakes.w: S-waves arrive first because they are stronger.
mistakes.r: P-waves arrive first because they are faster; S-waves often have larger amplitude but arrive later.

exam.q: State one difference between P-waves and S-waves.
model: P longitudinal, S transverse / P faster / P travels through liquids, S does not.

exam.q: Name the instrument used to detect seismic waves.
model: Seismometer (seismograph).
exam.tip: Spelling matters less than the idea.

exam.q: Explain why S-waves cannot travel through the outer core.
model: S-waves are transverse.
Transverse (seismic) waves cannot travel through liquids, and the outer core is liquid.

exam.q: Explain why the paths of seismic waves through the mantle are curved.
model: The speed of the waves changes gradually with depth (as density/properties change).
So the waves are continuously refracted.

exam.q: Explain what causes the P-wave shadow zone.
model: P-waves refract at the boundary between mantle and core.
Because their speed changes suddenly, so they are bent away from this region.

exam.q: A seismometer records P-waves 60 s before the S-waves arrive. Explain why the P-waves arrive first.
model: P-waves travel faster than S-waves.

exam.q: P-waves travel at 8 km/s. They take 150 s to reach a seismometer. Calculate the distance to the earthquake.
model: distance = speed x time = 8 x 150.

exam.q: A seismic P-wave has a frequency of 2.0 Hz and a wavelength of 3.5 km. Calculate its speed in m/s.
model: v = f x lambda = 2.0 x 3500.

exam.q: Describe how seismometers at three different locations can be used to find the epicentre of an earthquake.
model: Measure the time difference between P and S wave arrivals at each station.
Use the speeds to calculate the distance from each station.
Draw a circle of that radius around each station on a map.
The epicentre is where the three circles intersect.
exam.tip: Three circles meet at one point.

exam.q: Explain how observations of P-waves and S-waves provide evidence for the structure of the Earth's interior.
model: P-waves longitudinal, travel through solids and liquids; S-waves transverse, solids only.
S-waves not detected on the far side of the Earth (S-wave shadow zone).
So the outer core must be liquid; size of shadow zone gives size of core.
P-waves refract at mantle-core boundary producing P-wave shadow zones.
Curved paths show wave speed/properties change gradually with depth.
Faint P-waves in shadow zone suggest a solid inner core.
exam.tip: Pair each observation with its conclusion.

worked.q: P-waves travel at 8 km/s and S-waves at 4 km/s. At a seismometer the S-waves arrive 60 s after the P-waves. How far away is the earthquake?
steps: Let the distance be d km. Time for P = d / 8; time for S = d / 4.
Time difference: d/4 - d/8 = 60.
Check: P takes 60 s, S takes 120 s; difference 60 s.

worked.q: An S-wave travels 2250 km through the mantle in 5 minutes. Calculate its average speed in km/s.
steps: Convert time: 5 minutes = 5 x 60 = 300 s.
speed = distance / time = 2250 / 300.
speed = 7.5 km/s.

worked.q: Seismometers on the opposite side of the Earth to an earthquake detect P-waves but no S-waves. Explain what this tells scientists.
steps: S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through liquids.
P-waves are longitudinal and can travel through liquids.
The waves to the far side must pass through the core.
So part of the core must be liquid: the outer core.
worked.ans: It shows that the Earth's outer core is liquid, because it stops S-waves while letting P-waves pass.
